question: SQ-LIP-000012
text: Do hormones and heredity influence the onset of lipedema?
minor_problems: [minor] set: P5 (autosomal dominant pedigree pattern), P7 (heterogeneous rare variants 'rather than single-gene') and P8 (single-family AKR1C1 segregation) are in apparent tension in wording. They are reconcilable but the set does not say so.

[minor] set: The link between heredity and hormones, which is the heart of the question, is made only implicitly. E21's genetic correlations with leptin and age at menopause and E19's loci in hormone biosynthesis are not stated in a proposition, and E29/E15 suggest a hormone-pathway route on very thin data.

[minor] set: Reviews E10, E13, E24, E31 and E35 are correctly marked secondary_of E14, but the family-history figures from other primary sources (E11 46%, E22 60% to 80%, E17 30% to 89%) are not placed under P5, so the familial frequency range is under-represented.
[minor] set: Bookkeeping: E4 is an encyclopaedic entry (title about a male patient) graded 'moderate' and 'review', E19 is a preprint, and E2 has no quote.

[minor] P5: two ideas; misplaced ['E11'] — suggested: Lipedema frequently clusters in families, and pedigree studies suggest sex-limited autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance, although the pattern is not firmly established. (Bundles familial frequency (14.9% to 64% across sources) with inheritance mode, which is weaker, from one pedigree series (E14) re-reported by the reviews. Family history of 46% in E11 and 60% to 80% in E22 are not placed here. E9 counts affected relatives but does not test an inheritance model.)

[minor] P6: overgeneralized — suggested: Genome-wide studies suggest common genetic variants may contribute modestly to susceptibility to a lipedema-like phenotype, though findings are suggestive and await replication. (E21 uses an inferred phenotype in UK Biobank, not clinically diagnosed lipedema, and E18's locus is only suggestive (P 4x10^-6). The statement should say so. E19 is a preprint of E18, correctly secondary.)

[minor] P7: not fully supported; overgeneralized — suggested: Candidate variants appear to differ between lipedema families, suggesting possible genetic heterogeneity, though findings are exploratory and unreplicated. (Nine families and 31 individuals, with no functional validation. 'Rather than single-gene inheritance' sits uneasily beside P8 (AKR1C1 segregating in a family) and P5 (autosomal dominant pattern). Heterogeneity across families is compatible with both, so the contrast should be dropped.)

[minor] P8: not fully supported; overgeneralized; two ideas — suggested: Variants in steroid-metabolising genes such as AKR1C1 have been proposed as hereditary contributors to lipedema, based on limited family-level data. (One family with three affected members and in-silico (QSAR and molecular-dynamics) prediction of function, with no functional assay. The inference that heredity may act through hormone metabolism goes beyond a single segregation observation. The statement describes a study rather than a general proposition, and bundles segregation with mechanism.)

items.note: Narrative review explicitly describes hormonal triggers (puberty, pregnancy, menopause) and autosomal/X-linked dominant inheritance with family history in 16-64% of cases, directly supporting the affirmative; graded low because it is a narr
old_statements: This review reports that lipedema onset or exacerbation occurs during hormonal transition periods (puberty, pregnancy, menopause, hysterectomy/oophorectomy) with estrogen receptor imbalance (ER-alpha suppressed, ER-beta activated), and that it shows autosomal dominant or X-linked dominant inheritance with a family history in 16-64% of cases.

items.title: Lipedema: A Review of the Literature
items.quote: Histórico familiar positivo em 16–64% dos pacientes — herança X-linked dominante ou autossômica dominante com limitação por sexo
items.note: The review reports positive family history in 16–64% of patients with proposed hereditary inheritance patterns and onset in post-pubertal women, directly supporting hormonal and hereditary influence on lipedema onset, though as narrative re
old_statements: This review reports that lipedema onset or exacerbation occurs during hormonal transition periods (puberty, pregnancy, menopause, hysterectomy/oophorectomy) with estrogen receptor imbalance (ER-alpha suppressed, ER-beta activated), and that it shows autosomal dominant or X-linked dominant inheritance with a family history in 16-64% of cases.

propositions.statement: Lipedema onset or worsening is frequently reported at female hormonal transitions, especially puberty, and also pregnancy and menopause.
propositions.rationale: Surveys, cohorts, consensus and reviews consistently report onset clustering at hormonal transitions, though mostly by self-report.

evidence.finding: Brazilian Delphi consensus (113 experts) approved statements that hormonal factors (puberty, pregnancy, menopause) trigger or exacerbate lipedema (mean agreement 4.46), alongside a hereditary component.
Expert narrative review describing lipedema symptoms as closely linked to female hormonal transitions (puberty, pregnancy, menopause) on a polygenic predisposition.
In 115 patients with lower-limb edema, lipedema confirmed in 71%, all women; perceived triggers puberty 49%, pregnancy 22%, massive weight loss 22%; family history 46%.
Narrative review: onset associated with hormonal fluctuation periods, suggesting estrogen dependence (aromatase CYP19A1, estrogen-induced ZNF423 hyperproliferation).
Review: lipedema develops or worsens in hormonal-change windows; about 20% of cases identified at menopause and about 67% report symptom exacerbation at its onset.
Review: onset or exacerbation at puberty, pregnancy, menopause and hysterectomy/oophorectomy, with estrogen receptor imbalance; family history 16-64% cited from the pedigree literature.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Lipedema onset or worsening is frequently reported to coincide with female hormonal transitions such as puberty, pregnancy and menopause.

propositions.statement: Starting hormonal contraception is reported by some women to coincide with lipedema symptom onset or worsening.
propositions.rationale: Self-reported cross-sectional data and a case report link contraceptive initiation to symptoms, subject to recall bias.

evidence.finding: In 637 women with lipedema, perceived onset triggers: puberty 39.7%, contraceptive start 15.1%, pregnancy 11.6%, menopause 5.5%; 58.8% of contraceptive users reported worsening; recall bias noted.
Woman with lipedema reported worsening swelling and pain after starting oral contraceptives at 24, with partial improvement after stopping; family history of fat legs since adolescence.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Hormonal contraceptive use is reported to coincide with lipedema symptom onset or worsening in some women.

propositions.statement: Altered estrogen signalling in affected adipose tissue, including an imbalanced estrogen receptor pattern and local aromatase activity, is proposed as a lipedema mechanism.
propositions.rationale: Systematic and narrative reviews converge on estrogen-pathway hypotheses without direct tissue data among the items; the only controlled plasma measurement found no hormone difference (P4).

evidence.finding: Systematic review identified four hypotheses linking estrogen metabolism and receptor function, growth hormone imbalance and leptin-related stem cell changes to lipedema development.
Encyclopaedic entry reproducing the same systematic review conclusion: lipedema appears multifactorial, driven primarily by hormonal dysregulation, especially estrogen.
Review: estrogen-regulated polygenic disorder with onset at hormonal transitions, family aggregation in at least 16%, and an altered ERalpha/ERbeta pattern in white adipose tissue.
Narrative review emphasising estrogen: manifestation at puberty, pregnancy and menopause and a changed estrogen receptor alpha/beta distribution in adipose tissue.
Review proposing increased ERalpha/ERbeta ratio or local paracrine estrogen production in gluteofemoral adipocytes drives fat accumulation; cites exome variants in sex hormone genes.
Review: estrogen and its receptors (ERalpha, ERbeta, GPER) influence pathogenesis; reduced ERalpha and increased ERbeta in gluteofemoral fat parallel lipedema fat distribution.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Dysregulated estrogen signalling in adipose tissue, including altered estrogen receptor balance, is proposed as a mechanism of lipedema.

propositions.statement: Circulating testosterone and estradiol are reported not to differ between women with lipedema and controls, though evidence is limited.
propositions.rationale: A single systematic review found no plasma difference in these two hormones; E9 reports sex-hormone imbalance in some premenopausal patients but without controls, so it is not a direct contradiction.

evidence.finding: PRISMA systematic review of lipedema pathology: testosterone and estradiol showed no significant difference versus controls in plasma; etiology remains largely uncertain despite near-exclusive female occurrence.

propositions.statement: Lipedema frequently runs in families, in a pattern suggested to be sex-limited autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance.
propositions.rationale: The primary evidence is one pedigree series (E14) and one patient survey (E9); the reviews re-report the same pedigree data and are marked secondary.

evidence.finding: In 67 probands, 14.9% had an affected first-degree relative (all female); X-linkage excluded in the largest family (lod < -2), favouring sex-limited autosomal dominant inheritance; puberty onset in 55%.
Survey of 209 patients: affected grandmothers 35.4%, mothers 29.7%, aunts 23.0%, sisters 14.8%; mean onset age 16; 30.5% of premenopausal patients had sex-hormone imbalances.
Critical review citing the pedigree data (330 relatives): up to 60% of cases suggest autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance; proposes an estrogen-regulated polygenic disease.
Review re-reporting familial incidence in 15% of first-degree female relatives, consistent with X-linked or autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance.
Review: sex-limited autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance most likely; self-reported family history up to 64%; no confirmed gene for primary non-syndromic lipedema.
Review: up to 60% have an affected first-degree relative, sex-limited autosomal dominant pattern with incomplete penetrance, plus AKR1C1 and PIT1 mutations and estrogen pathway dysregulation.
Review: positive family history in 16-64% of patients, with X-linked dominant or sex-limited autosomal dominant inheritance proposed and post-pubertal onset.

propositions.statement: Genome-wide studies suggest common genetic variants may contribute modestly to lipedema susceptibility.
propositions.rationale: One genome-wide study used an inferred phenotype with low SNP heritability and the dedicated cohort found only suggestive loci; reviews re-reporting them are secondary.

evidence.finding: GWAS of an inferred lipedema phenotype in UK Biobank women: 18 genome-wide significant loci (RSPO3, GRB14-COBLL1, VEGFA, ADAMTS9), SNP heritability about 5.13%, correlations with leptin and age at menopause.
In a rigorously defined cohort (n=130), onset often followed hormonal changes; first dedicated GWAS found a suggestive locus upstream of LHFPL6 (OR 2.01, P 4x10^-6), replicated independently.
Preprint of the same cohort GWAS: only suggestive loci, top SNPs near lipoma formation, hormone biosynthesis and lipid hydroxylation genes.
Review re-reporting the dedicated lipedema GWAS (CPE, ZNF25, ZNF33A, linked to estrogen biology) and VEGFA, GRB14-COBLL1 loci; family history in 30-89% of cases.

propositions.statement: Lipedema may be genetically heterogeneous, with no single causal gene shared across affected families.
propositions.rationale: A family exome study found no gene shared across families; this concerns rare variants, distinct from the common-variant evidence in P6.

evidence.finding: Exome sequencing of 31 individuals from 9 families found candidate variants in 469 genes with none shared by all families, enriched in vasopressin receptor, microfibril and patched binding.
Editorial summarising the family exome study: 469 candidate variants, ontology pointing to vasopressin receptor, microfibril and patched binding, suggesting multigenic risk.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: Rare candidate variants differ between lipedema families, suggesting genetically heterogeneous rather than single-gene inheritance.

propositions.statement: Rare variants in hormone-metabolism genes such as AKR1C1 have been reported in isolated lipedema families, but replication is lacking.
propositions.rationale: Rests on one family with three affected members and an in silico predicted mechanism; the reviews re-report it.

evidence.finding: Exome sequencing in an autosomal dominant family: AKR1C1 p.L213Q present in all 3 affected (puberty onset) and absent in 9 unaffected members; predicted partial loss of progesterone catabolism.
Review re-reporting AKR1C1 L213Q segregating across three generations and proposing AKR1C enzymes, AKR1C2 variants and regulatory polymorphisms as a steroid-metabolism pathway in gluteofemoral fat.
Review re-reporting the familial AKR1C1 mutation (progesterone reduction), adding a PIT1 mutation (GH, prolactin, TSH-beta) in one sporadic case; 18 GWAS loci; 305 candidate genes sequenced.

propositions.statement_before_twin_merge: A rare variant in an aldo-keto reductase gene may segregate with lipedema in a family, suggesting heredity may act through hormone metabolism.

propositions.statement: Lipedema is reported almost exclusively in women.
propositions.rationale: Near-exclusive female occurrence is central to the hormonal hypothesis; the rare male cases with hormonal or hepatic disorders refine it.

evidence.finding: Narrative review: lipedema is almost exclusively found in women and typically begins during periods of hormonal change (puberty, pregnancy, menopause).
Male case report, only the third idiopathic male case known; two of three known male cases had hepatic or endocrine disorders, suggesting a hormonal route via peripheral aromatisation of androgens.

propositions.statement: Adipose-derived cells from lipedema may show upregulated adipogenic gene expression compared with controls of similar weight.
propositions.rationale: An in vitro expression finding, not a genetic variant, so it is kept apart from the heredity propositions.

evidence.finding: Cultured adipocytes from nonobese lipedema donors showed upregulated adipogenic gene expression versus nonobese controls; BMI also affected expression; other genes did not differ.

dropped.reason: Ultrasound imaging study that only mentions genetic and hormonal factors as background; reports no finding on hormones or heredity.

verdicts.note: Wording ('frequently reported') matches the evidence, which is survey, consensus and narrative-review material. Bookkeeping: the best primary onset data (E3 puberty 39.7%, pregnancy 11.6%, menopause 5.5%; E18; E14) are filed elsewhere, and E26 (about 20% at menopause) is inconsistent with E3. E2 has no quote. E34's finding text includes family history not relevant here.
A cross-sectional self-report study with recall bias plus one case report, worded 'in some women'. Adequate.

Worded as 'proposed', which fits reviews. E4 duplicates E5 and is correctly secondary_of E5. E8 (no difference in circulating estradiol) addresses systemic levels, not local signalling, so it does not conflict.
Hedged ('limited evidence'). E9 (30.5% of premenopausal patients with sex-hormone imbalance) is filed under P5 and pulls slightly the other way, but it is self-reported.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Lipedema frequently clusters in families, and pedigree studies suggest sex-limited autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance, although the pattern is not firmly established.
verdicts.note: Bundles familial frequency (14.9% to 64% across sources) with inheritance mode, which is weaker, from one pedigree series (E14) re-reported by the reviews. Family history of 46% in E11 and 60% to 80% in E22 are not placed here. E9 counts affected relatives but does not test an inheritance model.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Genome-wide studies suggest common genetic variants may contribute modestly to susceptibility to a lipedema-like phenotype, though findings are suggestive and await replication.
verdicts.note: E21 uses an inferred phenotype in UK Biobank, not clinically diagnosed lipedema, and E18's locus is only suggestive (P 4x10^-6). The statement should say so. E19 is a preprint of E18, correctly secondary.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Candidate variants appear to differ between lipedema families, suggesting possible genetic heterogeneity, though findings are exploratory and unreplicated.
verdicts.note: Nine families and 31 individuals, with no functional validation. 'Rather than single-gene inheritance' sits uneasily beside P8 (AKR1C1 segregating in a family) and P5 (autosomal dominant pattern). Heterogeneity across families is compatible with both, so the contrast should be dropped.

verdicts.suggested_statement: Variants in steroid-metabolising genes such as AKR1C1 have been proposed as hereditary contributors to lipedema, based on limited family-level data.
verdicts.note: One family with three affected members and in-silico (QSAR and molecular-dynamics) prediction of function, with no functional assay. The inference that heredity may act through hormone metabolism goes beyond a single segregation observation. The statement describes a study rather than a general proposition, and bundles segregation with mechanism.
Male case reports are handled correctly as refines. E12's hormonal-aromatisation interpretation is speculative, but the finding states it as suggestion.
In vitro, nonobese controls, hedged with 'may', context role. Relevance to hormones or heredity is indirect.

set_issues.issue: P5 (autosomal dominant pedigree pattern), P7 (heterogeneous rare variants 'rather than single-gene') and P8 (single-family AKR1C1 segregation) are in apparent tension in wording. They are reconcilable but the set does not say so.

The link between heredity and hormones, which is the heart of the question, is made only implicitly. E21's genetic correlations with leptin and age at menopause and E19's loci in hormone biosynthesis are not stated in a proposition, and E29/E15 suggest a hormone-pathway route on very thin data.

Reviews E10, E13, E24, E31 and E35 are correctly marked secondary_of E14, but the family-history figures from other primary sources (E11 46%, E22 60% to 80%, E17 30% to 89%) are not placed under P5, so the familial frequency range is under-represented.
Bookkeeping: E4 is an encyclopaedic entry (title about a male patient) graded 'moderate' and 'review', E19 is a preprint, and E2 has no quote.
